newsitem.title: UK: Drive opens to cleanse British politics of sleaze.
newsitem.headline: Drive opens to cleanse British politics of sleaze.

text.p: A campaign to cleanse British politics of corruption kicked off on Monday, but immediately ran into controversy over the identity of its main promoter.

The People's Trust, a non-political pressure group set up in January, said it had accepted a one million pound ($1.6 million) start-up donation from Mohamed Al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of Harrods store who is at the centre of a pre-election row over cash payments to members of parliament.
Fayed's spokesman Michael Cole is a director of the Trust, and his contribution was earmarked to fund a publicity drive.

"Poll after poll shows how people believes their MPs are sleazy and dishonest. That damages politics. We want to see a clean politics that serves people," Christopher Graffius, the other director of the People's Trust, told a news conference.
The People's Trust is asking all candidates in the May national election to give an assurance that they will not take paid consultancies if elected.
It said it would publish the names of those MPs who signed up to their declaration and those who did not.

"We have a corrupted political system...It is corrupted because it is a system which has ceased to serve the peoole and is instead serving the interest of (political) parties, which have ceased to be vehicles for political service and are instead conspiracies to secure power," Graffius said.

The drive was launched as a two-year-long "cash for questions" scandal, involving allegations that several Conservative MPs engaged in influence peddling, continued to dominate early campaigning for the May 1 election which the opposition Labour Party is favourite to win.
Fayed has said he made cash payments of tens of thousands of pounds to a number of Conservative MPs to represent his business interests in parliament during the 1980s.
Fayed was keen to see overturned an official trade ministry report criticising his takeover of Harrods.

Graffius insisted that the anti-sleaze campaign would not be compromised by the financial involvement of Al-Fayed, saying that the People's Trust was open about its funding, in contrast to the main political parties.
"Mr Al-Fayed has been very open about the fact that in the 1980s he paid MPs consultancy fees to represent him in the House of Commons...He is committed to cleaning up that culture."
"I don't see what he personally gains from (this campaign) at all," Graffius said.
He said the People's Trust believed Britons should be informed about whom their member of parliament intends to serve.
"I think most people want to be represented by an MP who gives all his time to his constituency and his voters and who doesn't give his time to serving corporate interests," he said.
